paper_title: What Makes a Good Symbol for Hybrid Discrete-Continuous Planning?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet robot planning often benefits from hybrid discrete-continuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes or discrete primitive actions. Existing methods typically rely on human-defined symbol sets or symbols derived from language supervision, without asking what makes a symbol computationally useful. In this paper, we take an inference-algorithm--centric view to define usefulness: a good symbol should expose the discrete commitments that simplify solving the original planning problem. We first introduce the concept of solver-sufficient symbolization by studying finite-horizon piecewise-affine systems, for which solver sufficiency can be precisely characterized, and develop a counterexample-guided algorithm for symbol invention. We then extend this principle to invent symbols for optimization objectives parameterized by general neural networks as energy functions, showing that solver-sufficient symbols can nevertheless be induced from their continuous optimization landscapes. Experiments on simulated and real-robot tasks show that the resulting symbols reduce solving cost while preserving solution quality, while also improving interpretability and steerability. Furthermore, our theoretical and algorithmic insights help explain why certain human-defined symbols are computationally useful.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet planning often benefits from hybrid discretecontinuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes in manipulation (e.g., fixed and sliding contacts) [11, 38] and symbolic relational states (e.g., holding, in) [19]. From resource-rational perspective in cognitive science, useful symbol can expose key commitments and abstract away details to support efficient planning under bounded computation [22, 30]: When person wants to go to the office with bag, the motion of the person and the bag must initially be considered jointly. Once the bag is being carried is established as symbolic commitment, the bags motion can be abstracted away when planning the persons path. While humans can invent symbols to reduce the complexity of decision-making, deep learning based solutions to decision-making often choose to encode the full decision landscape within single continuous-space model [12, 24]. They remove the need to declare discrete modes and dependencies priori, but fundamentally cannot remove the underlying combinatorial structure of the problem. For example, for neural-networkparameterized dynamics models, basins and barriers appear in the optimization landscape. This makes planning or optimization hard as tasks and horizons grow [17]. To this end, researchers have considered exposing symbol commitments explicitly as state variables, such as the object relation of person-carrying-bag, to break much of the global coupling in planning. The symbol invention problem studies inducing these symbols from data, but typically from predefined grammars and labels [2, 42]. Such symbols are often interpretable and descriptive, yet their construction typically relies on heuristics about the problem structure, such as sparsity and locality. As result, they may hinder rather than simplify planning. In this paper, we address this fundamental question: What makes symbol useful in hybrid discrete-continuous planning? 1 Our definition of useful symbol comes from the perspective of inference-time solving. We consider general family of hybrid discrete-continuous planning algorithms based on search-then-optimize [14, 21]: symbols partition the entire decision space into conditioned subproblems, within which continuous-space optimization is performed. Let denote all decision variables and the planning objective. Our goal is to solve the hybrid optimization problem: Let Φ : Ψ denote symbolization map, where each ψ Ψ is symbolic assignment. Fixing ψ induces the conditioned problem ψ joint : minxΦ1(ψ) h(xψ). This yields the decomposition: Pjoint : min xX h(x). In planning context, such symbols should decouple temporal and spatial dependencies that would otherwise require joint reasoning, allowing each grounded solve to involve only the local variables relevant to the selected symbolic commitment. To put these in practice, we begin with simple piecewise affine (PWA) systems [40], where the solver sufficiency and complexity can be studied exactly using TU-dimension tools [23]. We then extend this perspective to general settings involving neural networks, focusing on energy-based formulations which include frameworks such as diffusion and flow-matching policies [12, 32]. In both settings, we develop algorithms for both symbol invention and symbol-guided planning. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce solver-sufficient symbolization, in which symbolic commitments preserve optimality while reducing grounded solving cost. This formalizes the symbolic invention problem as an optimization problem rather than purely descriptive interface. We provide mathematical foundation for analyzing why certain human-defined concepts are useful in robotic planning, and characterize task hardness by the amount of irreducible discrete structure that must remain explicit for faithful solving. We develop and evaluate symbol invention and hybrid planning framework that retains key advantages of symbolic planning, including interpretability and behavior steerability. Overview of related work. In search-then-optimize planning [4, 21], the key step is to choose conditioned subproblem, such as mode assignments in MILPs [9, 36] and energy-based model inference with multi-seed initialization [12, 17]. This choice is hard because decisions are coupled. Researchers have formalized such coupling in AI planning problems [10, 35]. Hybrid discretecontinuous planners aim to address this by introducing symbols [18, 27], but their symbols come from labels or simple algebraic combinations of state variables [2, 42]. We instead derive symbols from the solver itself: the commitments required before make the conditioned problem cheap to solve, and the commitment number measures the problems coupling and irreducible combinatorial hardness. We include more comprehensive discussion of related work in Appendix A.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: In this section, we present extensive experimental results to answer the following questions: Q1. Can solver-sufficient symbols preserve optimality while reducing solving cost? Q2. Can solver-sufficient symbols explain why certain human-defined symbols are useful? Q3. Can solver-sufficient symbols retain the interpretability and steerability of symbolic planning? Experiment Setup. We evaluate our method extensively in both PWA (three 2D manipulation tasks and three in-hand reorientation tasks with multi-finger grippers) and network settings (three D3IL tasks to study symbolic structure discovery in multimodal decision landscapes [25], and two realworld tasks). Our task suites are shown in Fig. 5. The details can be found in Appendix F. Baselines. For PWA systems, we compare against solver-specific methods CoCo and GBD-MPC, which respectively predict discrete modes before applying convex optimization and refine the original problem through Benders cuts [8, 31] to accelerate solving. We also compare against existing symbol invention methods: PDDLStream with LLM-invented symbols, PGS, IVNTR, and pix2pred, which construct symbolic abstractions before grounded solving [3, 18, 28, 42]. The first accelerates the same MILP without symbols, and the second uses symbols not derived from the solver. For neural networkbased systems, we evaluate multimodal policies BESO, IBC, DDPM, ACT, and BeT under their energy-based variants [12, 17, 39, 41, 44]. PRESERVING OPTIMALITY WHILE REDUCING SOLVING COST We first evaluate solver sufficiency in the PWA setting using success rate (SR) and per-step inference-time speedup (IS). As shown in Table 1, our symbols largely preserve solution quality while reducing solving time. CoCo obtains efficient conditioned solves by fixing complete discrete assignments to construct an LP, but may exclude the optimum; in contrast, our method exposes only the commitments required for faithful relaxation, leaving the residual problem LP-solvable with lower-dimensional symbolic search  (Fig. 6)  . The remaining failures in our algorithm are mainly due to early commitments that invalidate successive transitions, caused by too-short planning horizon. For neural settings, we construct τ -descent-faithful symbols on top of trained DDPM policy without modifying its parameters. We report SR and descents-to-coverage (DCδ), the number of descents required to reach the τ -neighborhood of the global optimum with probability at least 1δ. As shown in Table 2, symbol-guided solving maintains high task success while substantially reducing DC103 , indicating that near-optimal solutions can be recovered with only few conditioned descents. Table 3 further illustrates that our CPR-invented symbols encode action-relevant commitments, whereas baseline symbols mainly describe state or geometry. Overall, our algorithms and results provide solver-centric interpretation of usefulness. 4.2 Q2. EXPLAINING THE UTILITY OF HUMAN-DEFINED SYMBOLS To investigate why certain human-defined symbols are computationally useful, we study MPushT, PushT variant in which four pushers simultaneously move T-shaped block to target pose. We manually construct nine MILP formulations containing 127 factors in total (Appendix F.3). We compute CPR symbolization for each formulation and evaluate each human-defined binary factor zi along two dimensions. Task necessity (TN) measures the decrease in task success when the factor is disabled. RETAINING SYMBOLIC INTERPRETABILITY AND STEERABILITY The invented symbols also enable steering at the level of motion preferences. As shown in Fig. 8, different manipulation strategies will emerge in policies trained for Aligning (pushing from inside versus outside), and Avoiding (passing an obstacle on the left versus right). These alternative strategies correspond to distinct basins of the underlying energy landscape hs, which CPR will discover as separate symbol regions. Because the symbol map is defined over (Eq. (5)), fixing symbol value ψ restricts the control command to the corresponding region Φ1(ψ). To make these regions interpretable, we use vision-language model to label rollout videos from different symbol regions and assign each region behavioral label. For example, the left basin in Fig. 8(a) is labeled pushing from outside. At inference time, we can manually set the symbol values associated with the desired preference. As shown in Table 4, this yields both high task success rates (SR) and high preference success rates (PR: the fraction of successful trials that also satisfy the preference). Discussion: horizon-induced symbol complexity. As the planning horizon grows, the decision landscape becomes more complex through accumulated long-horizon state-action dependencies, and the required symbol dimension generally increases  (Table 5)  . The growth may plateau once dominant modes are exposed. Yet the resulting increase in basin complexity also makes optimization harder, leading to moderate decline in SR. Tasks with clearer decision modes scale more favorably: for example, Avoiding, which mainly requires choosing passing direction around obstacles, needs far fewer symbols than Aligning. Limitations. So far, our formulation uses linear symbol models ux, which may be restrictive in some cases. Yet, if task-relevant modes are sufficiently abstracted and linearly separable in learned feature space, ux can still partition the landscape effectively; otherwise, nonlinear maps u(x) may be preferable. We include more discussions and ablation studies in Appendix E.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented an inference-algorithmcentric view of symbol invention: useful symbols expose discrete commitments that simplify planning. We formalized this principle for piecewise-affine systems and extended it to neural energy landscapes. Across simulated and real-robot tasks, the invented symbols reduce solving cost while preserving solution quality and provide an interpretable interface for behavior steering. These results connect symbolic abstraction to computational utility, offering basis for both inventing new symbols and understanding the usefulness of human-defined concepts.

sections.title: A RELATED WORKS
sections.content: A.1 SEARCH-THEN-OPTIMIZE: FROM MILP TO ENERGY-BASED MODELS Many planning methods share two-stage shape: commit to discrete quantity, then solve conditioned problem that is tractable once it is fixed. Optimization formalizes this as the partitioned optimization framework, where minimizing over partition indices recovers solutions of the original problem [4]. For piecewise-affine models written as MILPs, the index is the mode assignment and each conditioned problem is convex; methods differ in how that assignment is obtained, by warmstarting branch-and-bound [36], by predicting it so that convex program remains online [9], or by transferring Benders cuts across instances [31]. In each, the discrete structure is declared by the formulation and the effort goes into searching it faster; which partition to use, and whether the conditioned problem is tractable under it, remain open [4]. When the objective is learned network, the shape persists but no partition is declared. Energy-based and diffusion policies represent alternative valid behaviors as distinct basins of the learned objective [12, 17], and which basin run settles in is decided by its initialization. This is how multimodality is represented, not defect, but it makes the basin sampled rather than decided. Never represented as variable, it cannot be committed to or held fixed across successive solves. Adjacent action chunks, drawn from independent noise, may therefore select incompatible modes [6]. 13 Existing remedies act on the generated actions rather than on the basin: averaging overlapping predictions [44], selecting among candidates for consistency with previous decisions [33], or correcting the denoising process by inpainting [6]; each enforces agreement between consecutive outputs without making the basin explicit. We instead supply an explicit index together with what fixing it buys, at two strengths: for PWA systems the LP relaxation of each conditioned problem is exact (Proposition B.1), whereas for learned objectives one confined descent per region reaches within τ of the global optimum regardless of its start (Proposition B.4), certified from sampled descents and therefore one-sided over the continuous domain. A.2 SYMBOL INVENTION IN NEURO-SYMBOLIC PLANNING Symbol invention involves two questions: where candidates come from, and which to keep; existing methods differ mainly in the first. Symbols have been grounded in the preconditions and effects of given skills [27], taken as the discrete code of an autoencoder [1], tied to language vocabulary [34], enumerated from grammar over given object-centric features [13, 42], learned as neural classifiers supervised by operator effects [28], or proposed by pretrained vision-language model [2, 29]; with the set fixed, planners interleave symbolic search with continuous samplers [18]. In each case the admissible symbols are delimited before learning begins, by grammar, feature set, code size, or pretrained vocabulary. The second question is answered by measurement. Candidates are scored by the likelihood they assign to observed transitions [37], or by planning performance on distribution of training tasks under particular planner [42]. Such scores are informative but extrinsic: they report how symbol set behaved, not what fixing its value does to the remaining problem. They also do not single out set. The same task admits many symbol sets whose measured performance is close, and success rate then offers no basis for choosing among them. We take both the source and the criterion from the solver itself. Candidates are read off the structure that makes solving hardthe discretecontinuous interface for PWA systems, and the basins revealed by sampled descents for learned objectivesso no vocabulary is delimited in advance. The criterion is property of the conditioned problem rather than measurement: an exact LP relaxation for PWA systems, and, at the weaker strength that sampling permits, τ -descent faithfulness for learned objectives (Proposition B.4). The count is then itself measure of difficultythe commitments that cannot be relaxed awaywith the computable lower bound of Lemma 2.1. A.3 PLANNING EFFICIENCY AND STRUCTURAL COUPLING This paper is concerned with planning efficiency: what solve actually costs on given problem. Plan existence being PSPACE-hard in general [7], efficiency is studied through finer structural measures, separating along two axeshow many steps must be searched, and how much must be considered jointly at each step. In heuristic search these are the expansions to the goal and the branching kept at each expansion; Mao et al. [35] make the same separation explicit for relational policies, classifying problems by how policy circuits width and depth grow with object count and horizon. Work on the first axis replaces primitive steps with temporal abstractions [43]; work on the second prunes states whose novelty exceeds bound [20]. Both axes trace to one property: coupling among the decisions in planthe extent to which they cannot be made independently. Width notions make it operational: how many atoms must hold together before subgoal can be treated in isolation [10, 20], and the regression width of Mao et al. [35], + maxi ci, counts the conditions that must be maintained while subgoal is achieved. When subgoals serialize, search factors and both axes shrink; otherwise they must be decided jointly. The induced width of constraint graph measures the same thing [15]. All of these are defined on declared combinatorial structure: predicate vocabulary with preconditions and effects, or constraint graph. We measure coupling instead by whether the solvers relaxation is faithful using affine TU tools [5, 23] for PWA systems, sublevel persistence [16] for learned objectives. The two are not interchangeable: total unimodularity is not property of the constraint graph, since matrices with the same sparsity pattern can differ in it by sign alone. RATdim counts the commitments required before the LP relaxation is exact (Lemma 2.1), and fixing them 14 decouples the discrete and continuous sides; τ -descent faithfulness asks the same question where no transition structure is declared, with certificate established on sampled descents rather than exactly

sections.title: E FURTHER EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.content: E.1 BEYOND LINEAR SYMBOL AXES Whether linear partitions suffice depends on the feature space in which is expressed. When it is abstract enough that task-relevant modes are linearly separable, few cuts ux separate them; when basin boundaries are curved in it, linear cuts can only approximate them piecewise, and more directions are needed. We therefore examine whether richer symbol axes can better capture such nonlinear boundaries. For example, replacing the linear projection ux with quadratic form can reduce the required symbolic directions while improving success rate. However, increasingly expressive symbol functions transfer complexity from the network into the symbolic layer and weaken interpretability, limiting the value of higher-order representations. Figure 9: Quadratic Symbol Axes. It captures the curved decision boundary with fewer symbolic directions. E.2 ABLATIONS ON SOLVER RESOLUTION τ We vary the escape budget τ and report the discovered symbol dimension k, the fraction of conditioned regions that remain violating under τ -descent faithfulness, SR, and symbol-discovery time  (Table 6)  . The results support interpreting τ as solver resolution rather than fitted parameter. When τ falls below within-basin descent variation, CPR over-resolves noise, producing more symbols while leaving many regions unclosed. In an intermediate range, all regions close and decreases progressively with little loss in SR. Once τ exceeds the dominant inter-basin barriers, no explicit symbolic distinction is required (k = 0). Thus, τ can be selected from the empirical range between within-basin variation and inter-basin separation. E.3 ABLATIONS ON SAMPLING EVIDENCE. We next vary the evidence available to neural CPR through graph connectivity and descent initializations (Table 7; we take τ = 0.38, 600 optimization steps). With insufficient evidence, the inferred symbol dimension changes with the sampling configuration while many conditioned regions remain violating, indicating that the observed partition is not yet supported by the sampled landscape. Increasing the evidence budget progressively reduces the violating fraction, reaching zero with = 1 at 400 initializations. This trend highlights that symbol invention should be interpreted only after the sampled atlas closes: additional evidence resolves uncertain connectivity before the resulting symbolic partition is treated as stable.

sections.content: F.1 TASK REQUIREMENTS We evaluate six tasks (three 2D manipulation tasks, three in-hand reorientation tasks) with PWA objectives and five tasks (three D3IL tasks [25], two real-world tasks) with neural network settings. Task details can be found as follows. MPushT. 4 pushers translate and rotate planar T-shaped object. There are finite number of pushable points on each face. rollout succeeds when its position and orientation errors are below 0.15 and 0.15 rad, respectively. Hook. planar gripper manipulates finite-volume L-shaped hook to reach around and pull 0.318-wide square block toward divider. The task requires collision-free repositioning, establishing valid hookblock contact, and sustained pulling. Packing. The controller packs 48 randomly selected, heterogeneous rectangles into two stable support stacks inside one-sided shelf with 1.70 1.31 interior. Objects begin with randomized orientations and must respect spatial supports and constraints. Block. five-finger Shadow Hand reorients an 80 mm cube while maintaining feasible multi-finger grasp in the IsaacLab simulator. Its contact structure distinguishes five fingers and six object faces. Terminate when the rotational error is at most 0.10 rad. Cuboid. The Shadow Hand reorients 55 70 110 mm cuboid under the same fivefinger setting. Unlike the symmetric cube, its unequal dimensions make fingertip reachability and face transitions orientation dependent. Take 0.10 rad rotational-error tolerance. Pen. The hand reorients capsule-shaped pen of length 200 mm and diameter 16 mm. Contacts are organized across three finger roles and three axial pen regions, capturing both grasp redistribution and longitudinal contact changes. Take 0.10 rad success tolerance. Avoiding. planar robot endpoint traverses three obstacle levels containing one, two, and three obstacles, separated vertically by 0.18 m. The corresponding 2, 3, and 4 passage choices induce 24 collision-free route modes. Success requires crossing the goal line at = 0.35 without collision, within 250-step episode. Pushing. robot pushes two 30 mm boxes into two 50 mm target regions. Either colorpreserving or crossed assignment is accepted when both boxtarget center distances are at most 50 mm. Combining the two assignments with their two completion orders produces four distinct solution modes. Aligning. robot pushes planar object to randomized target pose from either its inner or outer side (two task modalities). Initial and target orientations span [90, 90]. Success requires position and orientation errors below 18 mm and 0.048π rad, respectively. Sorting. robot places multiple red and blue blocks of varying shapes into fixed colormatched baskets in arbitrary order. Success requires all blocks to be placed in the basket of the corresponding color. 21 Figure 10: MPushT Contact Domain. F.2 MILP SETUPS In this subsection, we summarize the MILP structure through its primitive discrete variables z, which define the mode and contact choices. We omit the continuous dynamics and full constraint matrices for space. We first outline the rules upon which our formulation is based, and then demonstrate the specific meaning of (Table 8 and Table 9). MPushT. T-shaped object is pushed to goal pose through 18 candidate contact points distributed over eight faces. Each binary factor zj activates unit push at contact cj along the inward face normal. Contacts on the same face are activated cumulatively to form contiguous pushing segments, with at most four faces active at each step  (Fig. 10)  . Hook. gripper manipulates hook to pull block toward divider wall. The 16 binary factors encode whether the hook is held, hookblock contact, their relative placement and facing surfaces, and whether the block can reach the wall within the current step  (Fig. 11)  . Shelf. Multiple objects are packed onto shelf through discrete pick-and-place primitives and we take 8 objects here as an example. The 41 factors consist of eight grasp actions, placements on the shelf floor, and stacking actions among objects. An object must be placed only on larger supporting object. Block. five-finger hand reorients cube through discrete fingerface contact graph. We denote that, ff: index finger; mf: middle finger; rf: ring finger; lf: little finger; th: thumb. The 20 factors represent active fingers, admissible fingerface assignments, contacted object faces, and one idle unit. Flow constraints allow multiple simultaneous contacts, with each active finger assigned to one face and no face contacted twice. Cuboid. The cuboid task uses the same 20-factor fingerface representation as Block. The unequal object dimensions change the continuous contact feasibility and reachable orientations, while the discrete factors retain the same finger, face, and fingerface semantics. Pen. five-finger hand reorients pen using three functional finger groupsopposition, medial, and ulnarand three axial contact zonesproximal, center, and distal. The 12 factors encode active groups, groupzone assignments, and occupied zones; two groups contact two distinct zones at each step.
